The Greater crested tern (Thalasseus bergii) is a large seabird distributed across tropical and subtropical coastlines of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Field studies conducted in colonies along the Great Barrier Reef indicate that eggs are incubated consistently at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that supports successful embryonic development. Under these conditions, hatching occurs after approximately 27.5 days [ab = approximately 27.5 days], a duration comparable to that of other larg at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]e-bodied terns. Newly hatched chicks weigh around 42.6 grams [Wwb = around 42.6 grams], a modest neonatal mass that reflects the semi-precocial developmental mode of this species. The initial wet weight of a newly hatched individual represents only a fraction of the adult body mass, highlighting the substantial growth trajectory that nestlings must complete before reaching independence. Parental provisioning during the early nestling period is intensive, with both adults foraging repeatedly to meet the energetic demands of the growing chick. This biparental care strategy is common among larids and appears essential for ensuring chick survival through the vulnerable first days after emergence from the egg.

Development of the downy chick proceeds rapidly during the first weeks of life, with feather growth and motor coordination progressing in tandem. Under the typical thermal conditions of this species (40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]), the age at fledging is approximately 39 days after hatching [tx = approximately 39 days after hatching], at which point the young bird achieves its first sustained flight. This milestone marks a critical transition in the life cycle, as fledglings begin to accompany adults on foraging trips while still receiving partial provisioning. Sexual maturation follows considerably later, with puberty estimated to occur at 117 days after hatching [tp = 117 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. The delay between fledging and reproductive maturity reflects the extended period required for young terns to develop the foraging skills, body condition, and social competence necessary for successful breeding. During this sub-adult phase, individuals may disperse widely across the species range, with some birds traveling hundreds of kilometers before returning to natal colonies to attempt their first breeding event. The physiological demands of migration and wintering further contribute to the prolonged maturation period observed in this species.

Reproductive effort in Thalasseus bergii is characterized by a conservative strategy typical of long-lived seabirds. Females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a fixed clutch size that is invariant across much of the species range. The maximum reproductive rate, observed in colonies experiencing optimal foraging conditions and stable thermal environments at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], results in approximately one clutch annually per breeding pair [F_R_i = approximately one clutch annually per breeding pair]. This low annual fecundity is balanced by high adult survival and extended reproductive lifespan, consistent with the slow life-history pace predicted for large Procellariiformes and Charadriiformes. The incubation period, during which the single egg is attended continuously by both parents, imposes substantial energetic costs on the breeding pair. Parents alternate between foraging trips and nest attendance, a strategy that minimizes egg predation risk while maintaining the thermal stability required for successful embryo development. Nest density within colonies can be high, leading to intraspecific competition for optimal nest sites and occasional chick mortality due to territorial disputes.

Body mass measurements from long-term monitoring programs on Lady Elliot Island reveal substantial sexual size dimorphism in adult Greater crested terns. The ultimate wet weight for males reaches approximately 305.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 305.7 grams], whereas females attain a lower asymptotic mass of around 241.7 grams [Wwi = around 241.7 grams]. This difference in adult body size likely reflects sexual selection pressures related to territorial defense and courtship displays, as larger males tend to secure more favorable nesting sites within dense colonies. The initial wet weight of a newly hatched chick is 60 grams [Ww0 = 60 grams], a value that represents the mass immediately after the down has dried. Growth rates during the nestling period are rapid, with chicks gaining up to 10 grams per day during the linear phase of development before fledging. These growth trajectories are influenced by local prey availability, with chicks in food-rich colonies attaining higher fledging masses than those in resource-limited areas. The observed variation in growth rates underscores the importance of oceanographic conditions and parental foraging efficiency in shaping juvenile development and subsequent survival probabilities.

Longevity records derived from banding studies indicate an impressive lifespan for this species. The maximum recorded lifespan under natural conditions is approximately 20.34 years [am = approximately 20.34 years], based on resightings of marked individuals in Australian colonies studied during the typical thermal regime of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of seabirds that exhibit delayed maturation and low annual reproductive output. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 2 years [tR = approximately 2 years], meaning that most individuals begin breeding during their third calendar year after hatching under colony temperatures averaging 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This deferred reproductive onset is a common life-history strategy among larids, allowing young birds to accumulate sufficient foraging experience and body reserves before committing to the energetic demands of egg production and chick rearing. The combination of extreme longevity and low fecundity makes the Greater crested tern particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic threats, including habitat degradation at nesting islands and shifts in prey availability driven by climate change. Population models suggest that even small reductions in adult survival can lead to rapid population declines, emphasizing the need for targeted conservation measures at key breeding sites.
